Initial translation ONLY of every supplied caption, no explanations.", "source_rows": [{"id": "en85-art-0008", "tag": "figcaption", "role": "historical_plate_caption", "text": "Frontispiece", "sha256": "605a8040a5845cfb9c6016ab763a8a13255f9fc450f63b4db44f47d29d1e743c", "native_leaf": 10, "asset_id": "phiz-0008", "source_caption_url": "https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/43111/pg43111-images.html", "emphasis_spans": 0, "bold_spans": 0, "smallcaps_spans": 0, "note_markers": []}, {"id": "en85-art-0041", "tag": "figcaption", "role": "historical_plate_caption", "text": "Our pew at church.", "sha256": "ba32fec41567d0fe455a7e9ee7cd6677a7c6749d720fa8d8565129450236e6b7", "native_leaf": 28, "asset_id": "phiz-0041", "source_caption_url": "https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/43111/pg43111-images.html", "emphasis_spans": 0, "bold_spans": 0, "smallcaps_spans": 0, "note_markers": [], "context_rows": [{"id": "en85-u004-b0007", "tag": "p", "role": "paragraph", "text": "Here is a long passage—what an enormous perspective I make of it!—leading from Peggotty’s kitchen to the front door. A dark store-room opens out of it, and that is a place to be run past at night; for I don’t know what may be among those tubs and jars and old tea-chests, when there is nobody in there with a dimly-burning light, letting a mouldy air come out of the door, in which there is the smell of soap, pickles, pepper, candles, and coffee, all at one whiff. Then there are the two parlours: the parlour in which we sit of an evening, my mother and I and Peggotty—for Peggotty is quite our companion, when her work is done and we are alone—and the best parlour where we sit on a Sunday; grandly, but not so comfortably. There is something of a doleful air about that room to me, for Peggotty has told me—I don’t know when, but apparently ages ago—about my father’s funeral, and the company having their black cloaks put on. One Sunday night my mother reads to Peggotty and me in there, how Lazarus was raised up from the dead. And I am so frightened that they are afterwards obliged to take me out of bed, and show me the quiet churchyard out of the bedroom window, with the dead all lying in their graves at rest, below the solemn moon.", "sha256": "8b61b31ff1fd77c995081678e16c510a0f95eb0f76adb48c59bf573cf7b1d057", "source_xpath": "/html/body/div[9]/p[7]", "emphasis_spans": 0, "bold_spans": 0, "smallcaps_spans": 0, "note_markers": [], "source_class": ""}, {"id": "en85-u004-b0008", "tag": "p", "role": "paragraph", "text": "There is nothing half so green that I know anywhere, as the grass of that churchyard; nothing half so shady as its trees; nothing half so quiet as its tombstones. The sheep are feeding there, when I kneel up, early in the morning, in my little bed in a closet within my mother’s room, to look out at it; and I see the red light shining on the sun-dial, and think within myself, ‘Is the sun-dial glad, I wonder, that it can tell the time again?’", "sha256": "af7a9c5ac41ad55e1f53ce085bc93d8c2499db86d556ac15cf004fe14dee6b04", "source_xpath": "/html/body/div[9]/p[8]", "emphasis_spans": 0, "bold_spans": 0, "smallcaps_spans": 0, "note_markers": [], "source_class": ""}, {"id": "en85-u004-b0009", "tag": "p", "role": "paragraph", "text": "Here is our pew in the church. What a high-backed pew! With a window near it, out of which our house can be seen, and IS seen many times during the morning’s service, by Peggotty, who likes to make herself as sure as she can that it’s not being robbed, or is not in flames. But though Peggotty’s eye wanders, she is much offended if mine does, and frowns to me, as I stand upon the seat, that I am to look at the clergyman. But I can’t always look at him—I know him without that white thing on, and I am afraid of his wondering why I stare so, and perhaps stopping the service to inquire—and what am I to do? It’s a dreadful thing to gape, but I must do something. I look at my mother, but she pretends not to see me. I look at a boy in the aisle, and he makes faces at me. I look at the sunlight coming in at the open door through the porch, and there I see a stray sheep—I don’t mean a sinner, but mutton—half making up his mind to come into the church. I feel that if I looked at him any longer, I might be tempted to say something out loud; and what would become of me then! I look up at the monumental tablets on the wall, and try to think of Mr. Bodgers late of this parish, and what the feelings of Mrs. Bodgers must have been, when affliction sore, long time Mr. Bodgers bore, and physicians were in vain. I wonder whether they called in Mr. Chillip, and he was in vain; and if so, how he likes to be reminded of it once a week. I look from Mr. Chillip, in his Sunday neckcloth, to the pulpit; and think what a good place it would be to play in, and what a castle it would make, with another boy coming up the stairs to attack it, and having the velvet cushion with the tassels thrown down on his head. In time my eyes gradually shut up; and, from seeming to hear the clergyman singing a drowsy song in the heat, I hear nothing, until I fall off the seat with a crash, and am taken out, more dead than alive, by Peggotty.", "sha256": "8452690e72d40d460e3fe7af38ef996ed1c26c6b192df69a651fef0da35aef42", "source_xpath": "/html/body/div[9]/p[10]", "emphasis_spans": 0, "bold_spans": 0, "smallcaps_spans": 0, "note_markers": [], "source_class": ""}], "context_instruction": "English context only; translate ONLY caption text; no body translation or literary review requested."}, {"id": "en85-art-0061", "tag": "figcaption", "role": "historical_plate_caption", "text": "I am hospitably received by Mr. Peggotty.", "sha256": "14c63d19d6f80a6a226c1e20ac72e66de84c587f106e817c4556ae30c95a7a53", "native_leaf": 31, "asset_id": "phiz-0061", "source_caption_url": "https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/43111/pg43111-images.html", "emphasis_spans": 0, "bold_spans": 0, "smallcaps_spans": 0, "note_markers": [], "context_rows": [{"id": "en85-u005-b0016", "tag": "p", "role": "paragraph", "text": "We were welcomed by a very civil woman in a white apron, whom I had seen curtseying at the door when I was on Ham’s back, about a quarter of a mile off. Likewise by a most beautiful little girl (or I thought her so) with a necklace of blue beads on, who wouldn’t let me kiss her when I offered to, but ran away and hid herself. By and by, when we had dined in a sumptuous manner off boiled dabs, melted butter, and potatoes, with a chop for me, a hairy man with a very good-natured face came home. As he called Peggotty ‘Lass’, and gave her a hearty smack on the cheek, I had no doubt, from the general propriety of her conduct, that he was her brother; and so he turned out—being presently introduced to me as Mr. Peggotty, the master of the house.", "sha256": "6241f4047e27b6a81f7195a2603ccb68e8c2e15039310f687827489a80b73d9a", "source_xpath": "/html/body/div[10]/p[16]", "emphasis_spans": 0, "bold_spans": 0, "smallcaps_spans": 0, "note_markers": [], "source_class": ""}, {"id": "en85-u005-b0017", "tag": "p", "role": "paragraph", "text": "‘Glad to see you, sir,’ said Mr. Peggotty. ‘You’ll find us rough, sir, but you’ll find us ready.’", "sha256": "d5dc8c562fcdaa05227feb074e15c1523539b60b4dc8f629eb9427aac3977d30", "source_xpath": "/html/body/div[10]/p[17]", "emphasis_spans": 0, "bold_spans": 0, "smallcaps_spans": 0, "note_markers": [], "source_class": ""}, {"id": "en85-u005-b0018", "tag": "p", "role": "paragraph", "text": "I thanked him, and replied that I was sure I should be happy in such a delightful place.", "sha256": "211d10a7814ccd29c066831e7aec9f864dfa9bc97273bdcbef24f726653a0912", "source_xpath": "/html/body/div[10]/p[19]", "emphasis_spans": 0, "bold_spans": 0, "smallcaps_spans": 0, "note_markers": [], "source_class": ""}], "context_instruction": "English context only; translate ONLY caption text; no body translation or literary review requested."}, {"id": "en85-art-0111", "tag": "figcaption", "role": "historical_plate_caption", "text": "My musical breakfast.", "sha256": "f5c0ff896994d6e1fde912d77597ee70060f6549c543efa933bc36588bd80574", "native_leaf": 66, "asset_id": "phiz-0111", "source_caption_url": "https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/43111/pg43111-images.html", "emphasis_spans": 0, "bold_spans": 0, "smallcaps_spans": 0, "note_markers": [], "context_rows": [{"id": "en85-u007-b0119", "tag": "p", "role": "paragraph", "text": "‘Yes,’ he returned.", "sha256": "a1662eaf9541dd7394339ac4bb97c629bfe085b8193328901fb20a39df7bbe64", "source_xpath": "/html/body/div[12]/p[120]", "emphasis_spans": 0, "bold_spans": 0, "smallcaps_spans": 0, "note_markers": [], "source_class": ""}, {"id": "en85-u007-b0120", "tag": "p", "role": "paragraph", "text": "‘Have a blow at it,’ said the old woman, coaxingly. ‘Do!’", "sha256": "1d3d7692a058af2d8aed8f9dd4837c4c4b6816a7ffc7049a151db743e97129fc", "source_xpath": "/html/body/div[12]/p[121]", "emphasis_spans": 0, "bold_spans": 0, "smallcaps_spans": 0, "note_markers": [], "source_class": ""}, {"id": "en85-u007-b0121", "tag": "p", "role": "paragraph", "text": "The Master, upon this, put his hand underneath the skirts of his coat, and brought out his flute in three pieces, which he screwed together, and began immediately to play. My impression is, after many years of consideration, that there never can have been anybody in the world who played worse. He made the most dismal sounds I have ever heard produced by any means, natural or artificial. I don’t know what the tunes were—if there were such things in the performance at all, which I doubt—but the influence of the strain upon me was, first, to make me think of all my sorrows until I could hardly keep my tears back; then to take away my appetite; and lastly, to make me so sleepy that I couldn’t keep my eyes open. They begin to close again, and I begin to nod, as the recollection rises fresh upon me. Once more the little room, with its open corner cupboard, and its square-backed chairs, and its angular little staircase leading to the room above, and its three peacock’s feathers displayed over the mantelpiece—I remember wondering when I first went in, what that peacock would have thought if he had known what his finery was doomed to come to—fades from before me, and I nod, and sleep. The flute becomes inaudible, the wheels of the coach are heard instead, and I am on my journey. The coach jolts, I wake with a start, and the flute has come back again, and the Master at Salem House is sitting with his legs crossed, playing it dolefully, while the old woman of the house looks on delighted. She fades in her turn, and he fades, and all fades, and there is no flute, no Master, no Salem House, no David Copperfield, no anything but heavy sleep.", "sha256": "2bad2b34745028b70508325f4bd50bf125e8c7b2019884bdb96777ebe32116ef", "source_xpath": "/html/body/div[12]/p[123]", "emphasis_spans": 0, "bold_spans": 0, "smallcaps_spans": 0, "note_markers": [], "source_class": ""}], "context_instruction": "English context only; translate ONLY caption text; no body translation or literary review requested."}, {"id": "en85-art-0101", "tag": "figcaption", "role": "historical_plate_caption", "text": "The friendly Waiter and I.", "sha256": "f2e11296e54fde9460da57ea6e5c408c679ced372f8a343d15459edc38a13e08", "native_leaf": 67, "asset_id": "phiz-0101", "source_caption_url": "https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/43111/pg43111-images.html", "emphasis_spans": 0, "bold_spans": 0, "smallcaps_spans": 0, "note_markers": [], "context_rows": [{"id": "en85-u007-b0062", "tag": "p", "role": "paragraph", "text": "‘Chops,’ I said.", "sha256": "1d8d9fe70f6b10100c03fbb3b910070d5164768609836e6cb6056d050f06d48b", "source_xpath": "/html/body/div[12]/p[62]", "emphasis_spans": 0, "bold_spans": 0, "smallcaps_spans": 0, "note_markers": [], "source_class": ""}, {"id": "en85-u007-b0063", "tag": "p", "role": "paragraph", "text": "‘Lord bless my soul!’ he exclaimed, ‘I didn’t know they were chops. Why, a chop’s the very thing to take off the bad effects of that beer! Ain’t it lucky?’", "sha256": "4a2c551e53ee46ca609de3850c5513a844ff84babc6ecb53dce413ff0f6d8f9d", "source_xpath": "/html/body/div[12]/p[63]", "emphasis_spans": 0, "bold_spans": 0, "smallcaps_spans": 0, "note_markers": [], "source_class": ""}, {"id": "en85-u007-b0064", "tag": "p", "role": "paragraph", "text": "So he took a chop by the bone in one hand, and a potato in the other, and ate away with a very good appetite, to my extreme satisfaction. He afterwards took another chop, and another potato; and after that, another chop and another potato. When we had done, he brought me a pudding, and having set it before me, seemed to ruminate, and to become absent in his mind for some moments.", "sha256": "02cb175f0bdb1339b84ef866cb6478cde420c1a8c6e2a7c1ab3eaef384ba1e7b", "source_xpath": "/html/body/div[12]/p[65]", "emphasis_spans": 0, "bold_spans": 0, "smallcaps_spans": 0, "note_markers": [], "source_class": ""}], "context_instruction": "English context only; translate ONLY caption text; no body translation or literary review requested."}, {"id": "en85-art-0151", "tag": "figcaption", "role": "historical_plate_caption", "text": "Changes at Home.", "sha256": "79cf03542dbf01911fd757af3385d2eb505f2d52f26e22c18b975855385565b7", "native_leaf": 102, "asset_id": "phiz-0151", "source_caption_url": "https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/43111/pg43111-images.html", "emphasis_spans": 0, "bold_spans": 0, "smallcaps_spans": 0, "note_markers": [], "context_rows": [{"id": "en85-u010-b0033", "tag": "p", "role": "paragraph", "text": "God knows how infantine the memory may have been, that was awakened within me by the sound of my mother’s voice in the old parlour, when I set foot in the hall. She was singing in a low tone. I think I must have lain in her arms, and heard her singing so to me when I was but a baby. The strain was new to me, and yet it was so old that it filled my heart brim-full; like a friend come back from a long absence.", "sha256": "f72e539a04045afefff2556cf1246120b78686bbb2b91de24f1c80b599897a06", "source_xpath": "/html/body/div[15]/p[33]", "emphasis_spans": 0, "bold_spans": 0, "smallcaps_spans": 0, "note_markers": [], "source_class": ""}, {"id": "en85-u010-b0034", "tag": "p", "role": "paragraph", "text": "I believed, from the solitary and thoughtful way in which my mother murmured her song, that she was alone. And I went softly into the room. She was sitting by the fire, suckling an infant, whose tiny hand she held against her neck. Her eyes were looking down upon its face, and she sat singing to it. I was so far right, that she had no other companion.", "sha256": "9ebc732e3b2dfbb9338751e8a1577ed1eef4112ed2a7ece204010b10538ed6bc", "source_xpath": "/html/body/div[15]/p[34]", "emphasis_spans": 0, "bold_spans": 0, "smallcaps_spans": 0, "note_markers": [], "source_class": ""}, {"id": "en85-u010-b0035", "tag": "p", "role": "paragraph", "text": "I spoke to her, and she started, and cried out. But seeing me, she called me her dear Davy, her own boy! and coming half across the room to meet me, kneeled down upon the ground and kissed me, and laid my head down on her bosom near the little creature that was nestling there, and put its hand to my lips.", "sha256": "84e7ddf0b3f160b6d5a339bf5f981af0e4235de3ad67f8f08c3e8dbac1c09164", "source_xpath": "/html/body/div[15]/p[36]", "emphasis_spans": 0, "bold_spans": 0, "smallcaps_spans": 0, "note_markers": [], "source_class": ""}], "context_instruction": "English context only; translate ONLY caption text; no body translation or literary review requested."}, {"id": "en85-art-0135", "tag": "figcaption", "role": "historical_plate_caption", "text": "Steerforth and Mr. Mell.", "sha256": "1d19879bc08dcc6c578e50bc8d64245b62e02221a25717c9ef06076f99031192", "native_leaf": 105, "asset_id": "phiz-0135", "source_caption_url": "https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/43111/pg43111-images.html", "emphasis_spans": 0, "bold_spans": 0, "smallcaps_spans": 0, "note_markers": [], "context_rows": [{"id": "en85-u009-b0036", "tag": "p", "role": "paragraph", "text": "‘Sit down,’ said Mr. Mell.", "sha256": "6b27aee3f04adf2645cc004c64276826da8dcbb6fe2246f8c2fd555b8baa3209", "source_xpath": "/html/body/div[14]/p[36]", "emphasis_spans": 0, "bold_spans": 0, "smallcaps_spans": 0, "note_markers": [], "source_class": ""}, {"id": "en85-u009-b0037", "tag": "p", "role": "paragraph", "text": "‘Sit down yourself,’ said Steerforth, ‘and mind your business.’", "sha256": "840bc761782037ca50536fa76229e63395f42a41c86aa95552fad14cefadba17", "source_xpath": "/html/body/div[14]/p[37]", "emphasis_spans": 0, "bold_spans": 0, "smallcaps_spans": 0, "note_markers": [], "source_class": ""}, {"id": "en85-u009-b0038", "tag": "p", "role": "paragraph", "text": "There was a titter, and some applause; but Mr. Mell was so white, that silence immediately succeeded; and one boy, who had darted out behind him to imitate his mother again, changed his mind, and pretended to want a pen mended.", "sha256": "6d4742b886eeeacd0395d78c9f793a73f341ecaaa4257ff9f8c694003982f672", "source_xpath": "/html/body/div[14]/p[39]", "emphasis_spans": 0, "bold_spans": 0, "smallcaps_spans": 0, "note_markers": [], "source_class": ""}], "context_instruction": "English context only; translate ONLY caption text; no body translation or literary review requested."}, {"id": "en85-art-0193", "tag": "figcaption", "role": "historical_plate_caption", "text": "Mrs. Gummidge casts a damp on our departure", "sha256": "0c779afbee256324258269ad4e280dd8d4630450a32e6ed0222ce4b13389d7b7", "native_leaf": 140, "asset_id": "phiz-0193", "source_caption_url": "https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/43111/pg43111-images.html", "emphasis_spans": 0, "bold_spans": 0, "smallcaps_spans": 0, "note_markers": [], "context_rows": [{"id": "en85-u012-b0112", "tag": "p", "role": "paragraph", "text": "But here Peggotty, who had been going about from one to another in a hurried way, kissing everybody, called out from the cart, in which we all were by this time (Em’ly and I on two little chairs, side by side), that Mrs. Gummidge must do it. So Mrs. Gummidge did it; and, I am sorry to relate, cast a damp upon the festive character of our departure, by immediately bursting into tears, and sinking subdued into the arms of Ham, with the declaration that she knowed she was a burden, and had better be carried to the House at once. Which I really thought was a sensible idea, that Ham might have acted on.", "sha256": "45fb04b42ed2e61d7a525251e56dd96b7365e60651d08ea38fde8c3f9677ee7f", "source_xpath": "/html/body/div[17]/p[112]", "emphasis_spans": 0, "bold_spans": 0, "smallcaps_spans": 0, "note_markers": [], "source_class": ""}, {"id": "en85-u012-b0113", "tag": "p", "role": "paragraph", "text": "Away we went, however, on our holiday excursion; and the first thing we did was to stop at a church, where Mr. Barkis tied the horse to some rails, and went in with Peggotty, leaving little Em’ly and me alone in the chaise. I took that occasion to put my arm round Em’ly’s waist, and propose that as I was going away so very soon now, we should determine to be very affectionate to one another, and very happy, all day. Little Em’ly consenting, and allowing me to kiss her, I became desperate; informing her, I recollect, that I never could love another, and that I was prepared to shed the blood of anybody who should aspire to her affections.", "sha256": "417c5fbadcd96c79d24bccab067563a6834d7c7fc0809773f1fbe0c06a07aa3c", "source_xpath": "/html/body/div[17]/p[113]", "emphasis_spans": 0, "bold_spans": 0, "smallcaps_spans": 0, "note_markers": [], "source_class": ""}, {"id": "en85-u012-b0114", "tag": "p", "role": "paragraph", "text": "How merry little Em’ly made herself about it! translate ONLY caption text; no body translation or literary review requested."}, {"id": "en85-art-0245", "tag": "figcaption", "role": "historical_plate_caption", "text": "I make myself known to my Aunt.", "sha256": "ad8da6dd46dd789bede95d140be40018e87a55580e160cc5dce87297ac62dcbf", "native_leaf": 178, "asset_id": "phiz-0245", "source_caption_url": "https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/43111/pg43111-images.html", "emphasis_spans": 0, "bold_spans": 0, "smallcaps_spans": 0, "note_markers": [], "context_rows": [{"id": "en85-u015-b0079", "tag": "p", "role": "paragraph", "text": "The unbroken stillness of the parlour window leading me to infer, after a while, that she was not there, I lifted up my eyes to the window above it, where I saw a florid, pleasant-looking gentleman, with a grey head, who shut up one eye in a grotesque manner, nodded his head at me several times, shook it at me as often, laughed, and went away.", "sha256": "2ccf8d3c3a32fa9c63619638051594467787b413c83ecbaee502f60331c37253", "source_xpath": "/html/body/div[20]/p[79]", "emphasis_spans": 0, "bold_spans": 0, "smallcaps_spans": 0, "note_markers": [], "source_class": ""}, {"id": "en85-u015-b0080", "tag": "p", "role": "paragraph", "text": "I had been discomposed enough before; It is enough that I place this boy under the eye of a friend of my own, in a respectable business; that it does not please him; that he runs away from it; makes himself a common vagabond about the country; and comes here, in rags, to appeal to you, Miss Trotwood. I wish to set before you, honourably, the exact consequences—so far as they are within my knowledge—of your abetting him in this appeal.’", "sha256": "eb6a3b45dbfd66850dafcefc00d81334c6ddc9f2a1721d88de59d6d41d576b9a", "source_xpath": "/html/body/div[21]/p[101]", "emphasis_spans": 0, "bold_spans": 0, "smallcaps_spans": 0, "note_markers": [], "source_class": ""}], "context_instruction": "English context only; translate ONLY caption text; no body translation or literary review requested."}, {"id": "en85-art-0305", "tag": "figcaption", "role": "historical_plate_caption", "text": "I return to the Doctor’s after the party.", "sha256": "15acd0ea05c4ed53222811796df36d9bc3c2057fb299663da2e77354c1d7305b", "native_leaf": 214, "asset_id": "phiz-0305", "source_caption_url": "https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/43111/pg43111-images.html", "emphasis_spans": 0, "bold_spans": 0, "smallcaps_spans": 0, "note_markers": [], "context_rows": [{"id": "en85-u018-b0166", "tag": "p", "role": "paragraph", "text": "We walked very slowly home, Mr. Wickfield, Agnes, and I—Agnes and I admiring the moonlight, and Mr. Wickfield scarcely raising his eyes from the ground. Delighted to be of any service to her, I ran back to fetch it.", "sha256": "40f368b141328eaaca113d119291f0715a01b5a66fccd0e2bfcaa68c8159d5a9", "source_xpath": "/html/body/div[23]/p[166]", "emphasis_spans": 0, "bold_spans": 0, "smallcaps_spans": 0, "note_markers": [], "source_class": ""}, {"id": "en85-u018-b0167", "tag": "p", "role": "paragraph", "text": "I went into the supper-room where it had been left, which was deserted and dark. But a door of communication between that and the Doctor’s study, where there was a light, being open, I passed on there, to say what I wanted, and to get a candle.", "sha256": "63adf7946ebce8468124ed780c74dc248f3e60f1b29bf5e549dd17ec569ebce2", "source_xpath": "/html/body/div[23]/p[167]", "emphasis_spans": 0, "bold_spans": 0, "smallcaps_spans": 0, "note_markers": [], "source_class": ""}, {"id": "en85-u018-b0168", "tag": "p", "role": "paragraph", "text": "The Doctor was sitting in his easy-chair by the fireside, and his young wife was on a stool at his feet. But with such a face as I never saw. It was so beautiful in its form, it was so ashy pale, it was so fixed in its abstraction, it was so full of a wild, sleep-walking, dreamy horror of I don’t know what. I shall esteem it an honour to be presented.’", "sha256": "d69d834761bb15dddee39630d794b97b4d1b329f05408b7fd690289954c44431", "source_xpath": "/html/body/div[24]/p[76]", "emphasis_spans": 0, "bold_spans": 0, "smallcaps_spans": 0, "note_markers": [], "source_class": ""}, {"id": "en85-u019-b0077", "tag": "p", "role": "paragraph", "text": "I could do no less, under these circumstances, than make Mr. Micawber known to Uriah Heep and his mother; which I accordingly did. When I booked my place at the coach office I had had ‘Box Seat’ written against the entry, and had given the book-keeper half-a-crown. I was got up in a special great-coat and shawl, expressly to do honour to that distinguished eminence; had glorified myself upon it a good deal; and had felt that I was a credit to the coach. I spoke from the pit of my stomach for the rest of the journey, but I felt completely extinguished, and dreadfully young.", "sha256": "eb2340ad5fac1d6ec818906bdd539809bafc3f8488c7e13e44228aac89b7a5f2", "source_xpath": "/html/body/div[26]/p[106]", "emphasis_spans": 0, "bold_spans": 0, "smallcaps_spans": 0, "note_markers": [], "source_class": ""}, {"id": "en85-u021-b0107", "tag": "p", "role": "paragraph", "text": "It was curious and interesting, nevertheless, to be sitting up there behind four horses: well educated, well dressed, and with plenty of money in my pocket; and to look out for the places where I had slept on my weary journey. When we clattered through the narrow street of Chatham, and I caught a glimpse, in passing, of the lane where the old monster lived who had bought my jacket, I stretched my neck eagerly to look for the place where I had sat, in the sun and in the shade, waiting for my money. When we came, at last, within a stage of London, and passed the veritable Salem House where Mr. Creakle had laid about him with a heavy hand, I would have given all I had, for lawful permission to get down and thrash him, and let all the boys out like so many caged sparrows.", "sha256": "a53013f05cdb8ad1d00304218c502e68e97f3b956c431151d47dd0c0a1f9c724", "source_xpath": "/html/body/div[26]/p[108]", "emphasis_spans": 0, "bold_spans": 0, "smallcaps_spans": 0, "note_markers": [], "source_class": ""}], "context_instruction": "English context only; translate ONLY caption text; no body translation or literary review requested."}, {"id": "en85-art-0379", "tag": "figcaption", "role": "historical_plate_caption", "text": "We arrive unexpectedly at Mr. Peggotty’s fireside.", "sha256": "a14542dd6fe774720248c844187c346c77f973a561b9713342f6e59bd18a8733", "native_leaf": 255, "asset_id": "phiz-0379", "source_caption_url": "https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/43111/pg43111-images.html", "emphasis_spans": 0, "bold_spans": 0, "smallcaps_spans": 0, "note_markers": [], "context_rows": [{"id": "en85-u023-b0120", "tag": "p", "role": "paragraph", "text": "The little picture was so instantaneously dissolved by our going in, that one might have doubted whether it had ever been. translate ONLY caption text; no body translation or literary review requested."}, {"id": "en85-art-20069", "tag": "figcaption", "role": "historical_plate_caption", "text": "My Aunt astonishes me.", "sha256": "48acb5ffaf6b956ec05fdac575be0be4ee9811a4cb906b980c859353f3907d22", "native_leaf": 404, "asset_id": "phiz-20069", "source_caption_url": "https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/43111/pg43111-images.html", "emphasis_spans": 0, "bold_spans": 0, "smallcaps_spans": 0, "note_markers": [], "context_rows": [{"id": "en85-u036-b0064", "tag": "p", "role": "paragraph", "text": "‘Thank you, Trot,’ replied my aunt, ‘I prefer to sit upon my property.’ Here my aunt looked hard at Mrs. Crupp, and observed, ‘We needn’t trouble you to wait, ma’am.’", "sha256": "f589522ca9ad219dac348f3ff7b522ec728b7d7294270069d44a75d9c90a608a", "source_xpath": "/html/body/div[41]/p[64]", "emphasis_spans": 0, "bold_spans": 0, "smallcaps_spans": 0, "note_markers": [], "source_class": ""}, {"id": "en85-u036-b0065", "tag": "p", "role": "paragraph", "text": "‘Shall I put a little more tea in the pot afore I go, ma’am?’ said Mrs. Crupp.", "sha256": "d27f83eaaa5fcc5b6a24fc12480d099e4f70ca7ed8a8ff80b96b884840c2eec5", "source_xpath": "/html/body/div[41]/p[65]", "emphasis_spans": 0, "bold_spans": 0, "smallcaps_spans": 0, "note_markers": [], "source_class": ""}, {"id": "en85-u036-b0066", "tag": "p", "role": "paragraph", "text": "‘No, I thank you, ma’am,’ replied my aunt.", "sha256": "60958aafc3e7814092578f603a2f2234efc23744773eb4880aba535567bfc33c", "source_xpath": "/html/body/div[41]/p[67]", "emphasis_spans": 0, "bold_spans": 0, "smallcaps_spans": 0, "note_markers": [], "source_class": ""}], "context_instruction": "English context only; I was prepared for a great change in him, after what I had heard from Agnes, but his appearance shocked me.", "sha256": "f30e600b30be55a4a88e3d61fd5c79a8cea171baeef24f633f6e2b161ec2e6c1", "source_xpath": "/html/body/div[42]/p[147]", "emphasis_spans": 0, "bold_spans": 0, "smallcaps_spans": 0, "note_markers": [], "source_class": ""}, {"id": "en85-u037-b0148", "tag": "p", "role": "paragraph", "text": "It was not that he looked many years older, though still dressed with the old scrupulous cleanliness; or that there was an unwholesome ruddiness upon his face; or that his eyes were full and bloodshot; or that there was a nervous trembling in his hand, the cause of which I knew, and had for some years seen at work. It was not that he had lost his good looks, or his old bearing of a gentleman—for that he had not—but the thing that struck me most, was, that with the evidences of his native superiority still upon him, he should submit himself to that crawling impersonation of meanness, Uriah Heep. The reversal of the two natures, in their relative positions, Uriah’s of power and Mr. Wickfield’s of dependence, was a sight more painful to me than I can express. If I had seen an Ape taking command of a Man, I should hardly have thought it a more degrading spectacle.", "sha256": "1dfd6a236a9b51a8bbd256ff3027d8d62c5f293bec2744c6ac1c22808e9fbb4a", "source_xpath": "/html/body/div[42]/p[148]", "emphasis_spans": 0, "bold_spans": 0, "smallcaps_spans": 0, "note_markers": [], "source_class": ""}, {"id": "en85-u037-b0149", "tag": "p", "role": "paragraph", "text": "He appeared to be only too conscious of it himself. After many compliments on this performance, we fell into some general conversation; and as I was too full of my desperate intentions to keep my altered circumstances to myself, I made them known to Mr. and Mrs. Micawber. I cannot express how extremely delighted they both were, by the idea of my aunt’s being in difficulties; and how comfortable and friendly it made them.", "sha256": "a17c008bf6f72bac0a2d8cf969d788ebd6453afd55ee027bfdf8f1700aa62782", "source_xpath": "/html/body/div[43]/p[111]", "emphasis_spans": 0, "bold_spans": 0, "smallcaps_spans": 0, "note_markers": [], "source_class": ""}, {"id": "en85-u038-b0112", "tag": "p", "role": "paragraph", "text": "When we were nearly come to the last round of the punch, I addressed myself to Traddles, and reminded him that we must not separate, without wishing our friends health, happiness, and success in their new career. Traddles imitated me in the first particular, but did not consider himself a sufficiently old friend to venture on the second.", "sha256": "b4a2216439ad42304b4365de5f40690619d4ad7e440016304c042f49222e8116", "source_xpath": "/html/body/div[43]/p[112]", "emphasis_spans": 0, "bold_spans": 0, "smallcaps_spans": 0, "note_markers": [], "source_class": ""}, {"id": "en85-u038-b0113", "tag": "p", "role": "paragraph", "text": "‘My dear Copperfield,’ said Mr. Micawber, rising with one of his thumbs in each of his waistcoat pockets, ‘the companion of my youth: if I may be allowed the expression—and my esteemed friend Traddles: if I may be permitted to call him so—will allow me, on the part of Mrs. Micawber, myself, and our offspring, to thank them in the warmest and most uncompromising terms for their good wishes. It may be expected that on the eve of a migration which will consign us to a perfectly new existence,’ Mr. Micawber spoke as if they were going five hundred thousand miles, ‘I should offer a few valedictory remarks to two such friends as I see before me. But all that I have to say in this way, I have said. Whatever station in society I may attain, through the medium of the learned profession of which I am about to become an unworthy member, I shall endeavour not to disgrace, and Mrs. Micawber will be safe to adorn. Under the temporary pressure of pecuniary liabilities, contracted with a view to their immediate liquidation, but remaining unliquidated through a combination of circumstances, I have been under the necessity of assuming a garb from which my natural instincts recoil—I allude to spectacles—and possessing myself of a cognomen, to which I can establish no legitimate pretensions. All I have to say on that score is, that the cloud has passed from the dreary scene, and the God of Day is once more high upon the mountain tops.
